concept.name: OpenID Connect Identity

relationships.description: Connects OpenID Connect Identity to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: An interoperable identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that issues cryptographically signed JWT ID Tokens so applications can verify who a user is.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use Authorization Code Flow with PKCE, validate the ID Token's signature via JWKS plus `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and `nonce`, and never treat an OAuth Access Token as proof of user identity.

concept.whyItMatters: OAuth 2.0 is strictly an *authorization* protocol—it tells a resource server what a token can access, not who the user is or how they authenticated. Before OpenID Connect (OIDC), every provider (Facebook, GitHub, Google) invented custom `/me` endpoints and ad-hoc token formats, creating widespread account-takeover bugs. OIDC standardizes authentication with a signed JSON Web Token (`id_token`), discovery metadata, and uniform claims.
whenToUse: Implementing Single Sign-On (SSO) across web, mobile, and SaaS apps using Identity Providers (IdPs) like Okta, Auth0, Keycloak, or Microsoft Entra ID.
Delegating user authentication, MFA, and passkey/WebAuthn handling to a hardened IdP instead of storing password hashes locally.
Federating enterprise B2B logins where each customer tenant brings their own IdP via standard OIDC discovery.
whenNotToUse: Machine-to-machine (M2M) microservice authentication with no human user—use OAuth 2.0 `client_credentials` grant or mTLS instead.
Legacy enterprise integrations that strictly mandate XML-based SAML 2.0 assertions without an OIDC broker.
High-throughput internal service-to-service authorization where opaque or stateless OAuth access tokens (without ID tokens) are sufficient.
keyPoints: OIDC extends OAuth 2.0 by adding the `openid` scope, which instructs the Authorization Server to return a signed JWT `id_token` alongside the `access_token`.
Always use the Authorization Code Flow with PKCE (RFC 7636)—even for confidential server-side clients—and never use the deprecated Implicit Flow (`response_type=id_token`).
Clients must validate the `id_token` signature using the IdP's public keys from `jwks_uri` (discovered via `/.well-known/openid-configuration`) and verify `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and `nonce`.
The `sub` (subject) claim—combined with `iss`—is the only immutable unique user identifier; never key user accounts solely on mutable `email` claims.
For SPAs, the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern keeps refresh tokens and access tokens in HTTP-only, `SameSite` cookies on the server rather than exposing them in browser `localStorage`.

examples.title: Multi-Tenant B2B SaaS SSO with Okta & Keycloak
examples.scenario: A B2B analytics platform needed to onboard 40+ enterprise customers, each requiring login through their corporate Okta or Entra ID tenant with MFA enforced.
examples.outcome: Implementing a BFF OIDC client using `/.well-known/openid-configuration` discovery per tenant reduced customer SSO onboarding from 2 weeks of custom SAML XML debugging to a 5-minute `client_id` + `issuer` form, while keying accounts on `(iss, sub)`.

examples.title: Migrating a React SPA from Implicit Flow to Auth Code + PKCE
examples.scenario: A consumer portal used OIDC Implicit Flow (`response_type=id_token token`), exposing JWTs in URL fragments, browser history, and `localStorage`, and failing Safari ITP silent-refresh checks.
examples.outcome: Moving to Authorization Code + PKCE behind a lightweight Node/Go BFF eliminated tokens from browser storage, enabled rotating refresh tokens (`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`), and cut session drop-offs by 68%.

tradeOffs.pro: Embedding `email`, `name`, and `roles` in the `id_token` avoids an extra network round-trip on login.
tradeOffs.con: Bloats JWT header/cookie size (risking 4KB/8KB HTTP header limits) and freezes claims until the next login.

tradeOffs.factor: Stateless JWT Validation vs. Token Introspection
tradeOffs.pro: Local JWKS signature verification takes <1ms with zero network calls to the IdP.
tradeOffs.con: Cannot immediately revoke a compromised `id_token` or `access_token` before `exp` unless paired with short TTLs (5–15 min) or a revocation list.

tradeOffs.factor: SPA Direct PKCE vs. BFF Pattern
tradeOffs.pro: Direct browser PKCE requires no server-side session store.
tradeOffs.con: Exposes tokens to XSS in browser memory/storage; BFF keeps all tokens server-side behind `HttpOnly` cookies.

failureModes.name: Missing `aud` or `iss` Validation (Token Confusion)
failureModes.description: An application verifies the JWT signature against Google's JWKS but forgets to check `aud == my_client_id`, allowing an attacker to replay an `id_token` issued for a different app.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a battle-tested OIDC library that strictly asserts `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `alg` (rejecting `alg: none` and `HS256` downgrade), and `nonce`.

failureModes.name: Keying Accounts on `email` Instead of `(iss, sub)`
failureModes.description: Users who change their corporate email lose access or, worse, an attacker registers a recycled email on a social IdP and hijacks the account.
failureModes.mitigation: Persist `(iss, sub)` as the canonical foreign key and treat `email` as a mutable display attribute (checking `email_verified: true`).

failureModes.name: JWKS Cache Miss Storm on Key Rotation
failureModes.description: When an IdP rotates its signing key (`kid`), clients with a 24-hour hardcoded JWKS cache reject all logins until the cache expires.
failureModes.mitigation: Cache JWKS for 1–6 hours, and on an unknown `kid`, trigger a rate-limited background refresh (e.g., max 1 fetch per 30s).

failureModes.name: CSRF / Login-Mixup Attack
failureModes.description: Omitting `state` or `nonce` allows an attacker to trick a victim's browser into binding the attacker's OIDC session to the victim's account.
failureModes.mitigation: Generate a cryptographically random `state` (bound to the user's pre-login cookie) and `nonce` (verified inside the returned `id_token`).

commonMistakes: Sending the `id_token` as an `Authorization: Bearer` header to backend resource APIs instead of using the `access_token`.
Accepting `alg: none` or blindly trusting the `alg` header inside an unverified JWT (allowing `RS256` -> `HS256` public-key confusion).
Storing refresh tokens in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`, making them trivial to exfiltrate via any third-party JS XSS.
Forgetting to validate `at_hash` when receiving both `id_token` and `access_token` from the authorization endpoint.
Hardcoding IdP endpoints instead of resolving them dynamically from `/.well-known/openid-configuration`.

sections.content:
## The idea

**OpenID Connect (OIDC) 1.0** is an identity layer built directly on top of OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749). While OAuth 2.0 delegates *access* to APIs via opaque or JWT access tokens, OIDC standardizes *authentication* by introducing a third token: the **ID Token**.

An ID Token is always a signed **JSON Web Token (JWT)** containing standardized claims about the authentication event itself—who authenticated (`sub`), which IdP vouched for them (`iss`), which client app the token was minted for (`aud`), when it expires (`exp`), and a replay-protection `nonce`.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through a modern **Authorization Code Flow with PKCE** for a web app using a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF):

1. **Login Initiation**: The BFF generates a 256-bit `code_verifier`, hashes it (`S256`) into `code_challenge`, and generates random `state` and `nonce` values stored in an `HttpOnly` session cookie. It redirects (`302`) the browser to the IdP's `authorization_endpoint` with `scope=openid profile email`.
2. **User Authentication**: The user completes password + WebAuthn MFA on the IdP's hosted domain.
3. **Authorization Code Callback**: The IdP redirects back to `/callback?code=abc123&state=...`. The BFF verifies `state` matches the cookie.
4. **Back-Channel Token Exchange**: The BFF sends a server-to-server `POST /token` with `code`, `client_secret`, and `code_verifier`. The IdP returns `id_token`, `access_token`, and `refresh_token`.
5. **Cryptographic Verification**: The BFF fetches the IdP's public key matching the JWT `kid` from `jwks_uri`, verifies the `RS256`/`ES256` signature, and checks `iss`, `aud`, `exp` (with <=60s clock skew), and `nonce`.

sections.content:
## ID Token vs. Access Token

Conflating these two tokens is the #1 OIDC architectural mistake:

- **ID Token**: Intended strictly for the **client application (Relying Party)**. Its `aud` is the `client_id`. It proves authentication occurred and carries identity claims (`sub`, `auth_time`, `amr`). Never forward it to downstream APIs as a bearer credential.
- **Access Token**: Intended for **Resource Servers (APIs)**. Its `aud` is the API identifier (e.g., `https://api.acme.com`). It may be an opaque string or a JWT (RFC 9068) carrying `scope` and permissions.

## OIDC grant flow comparison

| Flow | `response_type` | Security Posture | Token Exposure | Status in OAuth 2.1 / OIDC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Auth Code + PKCE (BFF)** | `code` | Highest (PKCE + client secret + `HttpOnly` cookie) | Zero tokens in browser | **Recommended default** |
| **Auth Code + PKCE (Native/SPA)** | `code` | High (PKCE prevents code interception) | Tokens in app/JS memory | Recommended for mobile/native |
| **Implicit Flow** | `id_token token` | Low (tokens in URL fragment & history) | Exposed to XSS & referrers | **Deprecated — avoid** |
| **Hybrid Flow** | `code id_token` | Moderate (complex validation: `c_hash`, `at_hash`) | ID token in front-channel | Niche legacy use only |

## Failure modes

1. **Cross-Client Token Replay**: Accepting an `id_token` signed by Google without verifying `aud == YOUR_CLIENT_ID` lets an attacker take a valid token from another app and log into yours.
2. **Clock Skew Rejections**: Distributed containers with 10–20 seconds of NTP drift can fail `iat` or `nbf` checks. Configure a bounded leeway (30–60 seconds), never unlimited.
3. **Broken Logout (`RP-Initiated Logout`)**: Clearing only the local BFF cookie leaves the IdP's SSO session alive, silently logging the user back in on the next click. Redirect to `end_session_endpoint` with `id_token_hint` when full sign-out is required.

## Handling JWKS key rotation cleanly

IdPs rotate asymmetric signing keys (`RS256` or `ES256`) every 30–90 days. A resilient verifier:

- Reads the JWT header's `kid` (Key ID) and looks it up in an in-memory JWKS cache (TTL 1–6 hours).
- If `kid` is missing from cache, performs **one** rate-limited refresh against `jwks_uri` (with a 30-second cooldown to prevent DoS amplification from forged `kid` headers).
- Pins allowed algorithms (`["RS256", "ES256"]`) explicitly in the verifier config so `alg: none` or `HS256` key-confusion payloads are rejected before signature math runs.

## Practical checklist

- **Use Auth Code + PKCE (`S256`)** for every interactive login; disable Implicit and Password (ROPC) grants on the IdP.
- **Verify all 5 core claims**: `iss` (exact match), `aud` (contains your `client_id`), `exp` (> now - 60s), `nonce` (matches session), and cryptographic signature.
- **Key users on `(iss, sub)`**: Never use `email` as a primary key.
- **Keep tokens server-side**: Prefer a BFF with `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` session cookies for browser apps.
- **Implement `kid`-miss JWKS refresh** with a rate-limit guard so key rotations never cause login outages.

interviewProblems.title: OpenID Connect Identity
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on OpenID Connect Identity. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: An interoperable identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that issues cryptographically signed JWT ID Tokens so applications can verify who a user is.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: OIDC Identity Provider applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Discovery & JWKS.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Discovery & JWKS experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use a battle-tested OIDC library that strictly asserts `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `alg` (rejecting `alg: none` and `HS256` downgrade), and `nonce`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use Authorization Code Flow with PKCE, validate the ID Token's signature via JWKS plus `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and `nonce`, and never treat an OAuth Access Token as proof of user identity.
Avoid trap: Sending the `id_token` as an `Authorization: Bearer` header to backend resource APIs instead of using the `access_token`.
Avoid trap: Accepting `alg: none` or blindly trusting the `alg` header inside an unverified JWT (allowing `RS256` -> `HS256` public-key confusion).
When to reach for it: Implementing Single Sign-On (SSO) across web, mobile, and SaaS apps using Identity Providers (IdPs) like Okta, Auth0, Keycloak, or Microsoft Entra ID.
When to reach for it: Delegating user authentication, MFA, and passkey/WebAuthn handling to a hardened IdP instead of storing password hashes locally.

putItTogether.title: Putting Openid Connect Identity Together
putItTogether.summary: Use Authorization Code Flow with PKCE, validate the ID Token's signature via JWKS plus `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and `nonce`, and never treat an OAuth Access Token as proof of user identity.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Openid Connect Identity before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Implementing a BFF OIDC client using `/.well-known/openid-configuration` discovery per tenant reduced customer SSO onboarding from 2 weeks of custom SAML XML debugging to a 5-minute `client_id` + `issuer` form, while keying accounts on `(iss, sub)`.
